title: Mohnish Pabrai’s Q&A session at the Harvard Business School on September 15, 2023
summary: A wide-ranging Q&A with HBS students covering the 'Heads I win, tails I don't lose much' framework as the way non-venture-backed entrepreneurs (the barber, the Patels, his own IT business) minimize risk, his transition from CEO to running Pabrai Funds as a Buffett-partnership clone, and his Turkish investments as 'hundred-dollar bills on the ground'. He also discusses concentration versus diversification, the Buffett lunch and friendship with Munger, Dakshana's measurement-driven philanthropy, surrounding yourself with givers, the origin of Buffett closing his partnership, and avoiding leverage.

ideas.idea: Entrepreneurs are not risk-takers; non-venture-backed startups succeed by doing everything possible to minimize risk, which is the 'Heads I win, tails I don't lose much' framework.
ideas.detail: Non-venture-backed startups are 99.999% of all startups. His barber example: a barber sublets a small space one day a week in a new town 10-15 miles away, using used equipment and no payroll, so the downside is tiny while the upside is super-normal profits if the town booms.

ideas.idea: The Patels became low-cost providers by accident and turned a non-durable advantage into a 50-year dominance of the US motel industry.
ideas.detail: Expelled from Uganda by Idi Amin, they lived in the motel, employed the whole family, had a bank finance 70-90% of the purchase, charged 10-15% less than competitors and ran near 100% occupancy. Though under 0.1% of the US population, they own around 50% of all motels and are creeping to 15-25% of higher-end hotels.

ideas.idea: In value investing the very first thing is downside protection; you don't even look at the upside until you have looked at the downside.
ideas.detail: Like the barber who scrounges to keep risk down rather than signing a fancy lease, investors look for free lunches where downside is near zero and upside is massive. Auction-driven markets overshoot and undershoot, so hated and unloved things get mispriced in the right direction; 'we don't need to go buy Nvidia'.

ideas.idea: Start a business on the side while keeping your job, calibrating your effort at work to stay just above firing level so the paycheck keeps coming.
ideas.detail: For nine months he worked about 80 hours a week on his IT consulting startup while employed, deliberately no longer caring about great reviews. After nine months he had three clients and more cash flow than his paycheck; his bosses later admitted they had discussed firing him but concluded it wasn't bad enough, and both later invested in Pabrai Funds.

ideas.idea: His only 'employer' throughout his career has been the minimization of risk; scroungy startups that take no capital worked, while professionally resourced ventures all failed.
ideas.detail: First business cost $500-600 and went nowhere, the second about $2,000 and six months part-time. The third took $30,000 from his 401K at age 25 and about $70,000 of maxed-out credit cards, but was already profitable with clients when the money went in; it reached about $20 million in revenue and was sold in 2000.

ideas.idea: Applying Buffett's approach to a million dollars from a partial business sale in 1994 turned it into about $13 million in five or six years, roughly a 70% annualized return, which pulled him toward investing and away from being a CEO.
ideas.detail: He applied to Buffett for a job in 1999 and was told 'I work alone', so friends who had followed his stock tips since 1994 asked him to manage their money. Pabrai Investment Funds started in July 1999 as a hobby with about $1 million from eight friends plus $100,000 of his own; he now manages around $900 million.

ideas.idea: A simple '10 by 10' portfolio, about ten stocks at one-tenth of assets each held until they reach intrinsic value, works because investing is forgiving even if you are wrong half the time.
ideas.detail: This was his personal approach from 1994 to 1999, investing only in public markets and waiting for positions to reach intrinsic value.

ideas.idea: In the 2000 bubble he was buying funeral homes at two times earnings, steel and coal companies while everyone else bought Pets.com, so the fund was up about 70% by June 2000 while the Nasdaq crashed.
ideas.detail: Coke traded at 50 times earnings and Microsoft at a $600-700 billion market cap it did not see again for 10-11 years, giving seriously negative returns for 10-12 years. He switched from tech investing in the 1990s to hard-core Ben Graham deep value in early 2000 because it was the only thing that made sense.

ideas.idea: Excel-based finance education, CAPM and efficient market theory fill your head with mush; you should detox and never need Excel again.
ideas.detail: These models are beautiful to play with in Excel but have nothing to do with how the world works. Very few business schools (Columbia, Florida, Missouri, Jack McDonald at Stanford) teach Buffett's approach, and Harvard has no strong value investing program.

ideas.idea: Humans have an inexplicable aversion to cloning, so great ideas like the Buffett partnership structure or the Chipotle format go unreplicated for decades, leaving huge opportunity for the shameless cloner.
ideas.detail: Buffett ran his partnerships from 1956 to 1969 with no management fee and one-fourth of the upside over 6%; nobody visible replicated it until Pabrai in 1999, 30 years later, and Munger confirmed only a couple of obscure people had. Chipotle's user-directed assembly format is not rocket science yet took years before CAVA and others copied it.

ideas.idea: The complete Buffett education is free: about 150 hours of Berkshire annual meetings on buffett.cnbc.com plus the letters and transcripts, yet almost no one is interested.
ideas.detail: He listened to every annual meeting from the past 25-plus years twice while showering and shaving each morning, taking six or seven months per pass, and is on his third pass, currently in the 2001 afternoon session, learning more each time.

ideas.idea: Owners of private businesses hold 90-95% of their net worth in one illiquid company and are perfectly comfortable, so in public markets going beyond roughly 5-10 stocks only hurts you.
ideas.detail: You will not know the 11th business as well as your second-best business, so why buy the 11th instead of more of the second. He held more than 90-95% of his own net worth in his third startup for a long time, like the Chinese-restaurant couple or the barber.

ideas.idea: Turkey was a poker game against blindfolded players: foreign investors had all left and local investors are gamblers whose float turns over completely every nine days.
ideas.topic: Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US
ideas.detail: Of 200-300 listed Turkish companies, excluding promoter stakes, the entire float changes hands roughly every nine days. He invokes Buffett's line that the stock market transfers wealth from the active to the inactive. He owns three Turkish businesses: a warehouse operator, a Coke bottler and an airport operator, all widely mispriced.

ideas.idea: The Turkish warehouse operator traded at 2% of liquidation value in 2019, a $16 million market cap against about $800 million of net asset value that took 20 minutes to compute.
ideas.detail: Warehouses worth about $1 billion leased 99% on 10-year inflation-indexed leases to Amazon, IKEA, Carrefour, Mercedes, Toyota and DuPont, with $200 million of debt. He got one-third of the company for about $8 million; Templeton sold him a 5% block for $1 million. By 2023 the market cap exceeded $700 million and the business is worth about $1.5 billion even though the lira fell from 5 to 28 per dollar.

ideas.idea: Paying over $650,000 for the Buffett lunch was a cheap tuition bill; he was willing to bid $2 million, about 3% of the wealth he had made by cloning Buffett, and his only agenda was to say thank you.
ideas.detail: In 2007 he was worth about $85 million, most of it from plagiarizing Buffett. Guy Spier joined capped at $250,000 for two seats. The agenda-free lunch led to a friendship with Munger, whom he enjoyed even more, and standing invitations to Buffett's Sunday brunch with directors and celebrities; the last lunch went for about $19 million.

ideas.idea: Because wealth compounds beyond what he can spend, he runs two games: a wealth-accumulation engine and a wealth-disbursement engine, aiming for a net worth near zero on June 10, 2054, the day before he expects to leave the planet.
ideas.detail: Even at 10% a year, rule of 72 over 31 years means four or five doublings, about 32x, all of which must be given away optimally. He cites 'The Billionaire Who Wasn't' (Chuck Feeney) who lives on $5,000-6,000 a month in a rented condo as the model.

ideas.idea: Using Munger's inversion, he only funds causes where social return on invested capital can be measured easily, which led Dakshana to IIT entrance-exam coaching for poor rural kids.
ideas.detail: In 2005-2006 he could not find a single nonprofit that measured outcomes. IIT prep costs $5,000-6,000 for a 1.3% admit rate (2 million applicants for 13,000 seats), impossible for families earning $300-600 a year. Dakshana has seven campuses, the largest 109 acres, an unmanipulable third-party report card each year, and after 16 years is tuning the model like time spent on thermodynamics versus organic chemistry; eventually alumni will run it entirely.

ideas.idea: He is fundamentally a game player who only plays games where he has an edge: bridge, blackjack, investing and philanthropy, and all of them must be fun.
ideas.detail: Psychologists who profiled him concluded he likes games he thinks he can win. He has no blueprint for the next investment or where Dakshana will be in five years; if things are fun they get done well.

ideas.idea: When there is purity of purpose the universe conspires to help you; be a giver and ruthlessly eliminate takers and matchers from your life.
ideas.detail: Citing Adam Grant's 'Give and Take', givers end up receiving ten times more, as with the agenda-free Buffett lunch. Dakshana should have failed in India but worked because the team was purer of purpose than he was. He deliberately befriended Munger's Friday bridge circle because they were the highest quality people he had ever met and all givers; we become who we spend time with.

ideas.idea: Buffett closed his partnership in 1969-70 because markets were extremely overheated and he could find nothing to buy, which left him with dry powder to 'kill it' after the 1973-74 crash.
ideas.detail: Buffett was worth $25-30 million (over $200 million today) at around age 40 and rolled his stake into Berkshire. Munger kept his partnership and got clobbered in the 60-70% slow-motion crash of 1973-74, ending it in 1974. Buffett went from a 'sex-starved man on a deserted island' in 1969 to 'in a harem' in 1975; 1975-81 and the 1980s were incredible periods. Buffett says most of the interesting things in his life happened after age 47.

ideas.idea: Never selling winners is how the Davis family got rich: 98% of Grandfather Davis's insurance portfolio did nothing, but the 2% in AIG became 95% of the pie.
ideas.detail: Davis bought a gazillion mostly mediocre insurance companies in the 1930s and never sold anything; AIG, bought when it was a tiny Shanghai insurer, grew north of a $100 billion market cap. Chris Davis, the third generation, now sits on Berkshire's board.

ideas.idea: His biggest career mistake has been repeatedly selling great businesses too soon; concentration is the only way to build wealth, and once independently wealthy taking some chips off the table is forgivable but holding great businesses is better.
ideas.detail: The Turkish warehouse operator is already more than 60% of one of his funds and he tells investors every quarter to leave if uncomfortable. He hopes to hold the Coke bottler (a dozen countries plus the number one beer brand in another dozen) and the airport operator for a very long time. Still, capitalism is brutal and no business survives forever; the oldest is a 700-year-old hotel in Kyoto, and he would not fault the Waltons for putting half into the S&P 500.

ideas.idea: Charlie Munger asks the best questions and insists you have no business holding an opinion unless you can state the other side just as eloquently; rereading 'The Psychology of Human Misjudgment' each year gives a big edge.
ideas.detail: Munger attributes his success to being rational, and answers Dakshana fork-in-the-road questions before Pabrai finishes articulating them despite never visiting India. Our brains are a mishmash of ancient and modern wiring, so understanding those quirks is a leg up; Poor Charlie's Almanack is the book to read.

ideas.idea: Munger is the architect of Berkshire and Buffett the general contractor; Munger's willingness to be number two to Buffett shows the power of his mind, and he was right about paying up for Costco long before Buffett.
ideas.detail: Munger asked 'why wouldn't I want to be number two to Warren Buffett?' Buffett's hijacker joke ends with Munger wanting to talk once more about Costco and Buffett saying 'shoot me first'; Buffett now regrets never taking a Costco stake. They have disagreed many times but never had a real argument.

ideas.idea: If you are buying assets at pennies on the dollar you should not need leverage; avoid leverage in life and prefer businesses with zero debt so they can play offense in downturns.
ideas.detail: Something at one-fifth of liquidation value gives great returns unlevered, and levered thinking clouds judgment. He recommends Pulak Prasad's 2023 book 'What I Learned About Investing from Darwin': Prasad's fund and all its portfolio companies carry zero leverage because leveraged businesses lose optionality in downturns. Non-recourse structures are the only acceptable exception when starting out.
